claim: Latent WM-reasoning correlation is high but not 1: K&C 1990 reported .80-.90 (four USAF samples, shared arithmetic content); Kane et al 2005 median .72 over 14 datasets (>3,100 people, about 50% shared variance); Conway et al 2002 .60; Ackerman 2005 true-score WM-g .479 over 86 samples.
agent_test: Prior only: capacity explains roughly half of reasoning variance, not all
audit_note: Ackerman is given as r=.48 (CI .44-.52) in the opened source, not .479; Kane 2005 median .72 over 14 datasets and >3,100 subjects confirmed on PubMed abstract.

claim: The strongest headline (.80-.90) may be partly inflated by content overlap (an arithmetic reasoning test in all four samples) and an arbitrary, impure WM battery; later latent-variable studies with other designs report lower values (.58-.72), though the sources do not establish those designs were free of overlap.
agent_test: Run rule-holding tests with content-matched vs content-different load tasks and compare correlation
audit_note: Sources say the .80-.90 may be partly due to arithmetic content overlap and an arbitrary battery (K and C conceded arbitrariness); they do not show it was inflated, nor that .58-.72 come from overlap-free designs.
claim_before_audit: The strongest headline (.80-.90) is inflated by content overlap (arithmetic reasoning in all four samples) and task-impure batteries; designs without overlap give .58-.72.

claim: Complex span (storage plus processing) predicts Gf; simple span (digit/word span) does not. Complex-span alphas .70-.80, intercorrelations .40-.60.
agent_test: Compare agent accuracy when it must hold plus transform vs only repeat items

claim: In one Sternberg-scan variant reviewed by Conway, Kane and Engle (2003), low-WMC people had steeper RT slopes than high-WMC people only when letters overlapped across sets; with no overlap slopes did not differ. This is one example, and it suggests (not shows) that capacity matters most under interference.
schema_part: G (limit live rules); O distractor pruning
agent_test: Vary overlap of rules at fixed rule count; measure accuracy slope
audit_note: Only Conway et al. (one Sternberg-variant study) supports the overlap-specific slope result; the second source (Little et al. 2014) is about item difficulty, not interference, and the general rule is extrapolated from one example.
claim_before_audit: Capacity matters most where there is interference/overlap: low-WMC people have steeper slopes only when items overlap; with no overlap slopes did not differ.

claim: Rule count drives Raven item difficulty (Carpenter 1990: rule tokens explain 57% of item variance), but whether the WM-Raven link is item-invariant is disputed; Little 2014 simulations show invariance tests have low power at moderate r. I-RAVEN-X (Hersche 2024) varies grid length and value range, not rule count, so it does not test this; the LLM drop there tracks arithmetic rules and number magnitude.
agent_test: Score agent on matrix items sorted by rule tokens; check if the decline tracks token count

claim: WM-Gf correlation depends on speeding: with unspeeded long testing WM explained about 38% of variance (Chuderski 2013, blog-summary level source only).
agent_test: Vary token budget on the same items and watch the load effect

claim: Attention control (antisaccade, visual arrays) may carry much of the WM-Gf link (Draheim 2021, N=396: full latent mediation only with reliable accuracy-based tasks, not yet replicated); attention restraint and attention constraint are correlated but separable (Kane 2016, 95% CI around the correlation .46 to .74, which excludes 1.0).
agent_test: Test whether adding a distractor-suppression step helps at equal tokens
audit_note: In Kane et al. 2016 [.46,.74] is the 95% confidence interval around one correlation (attention restraint with attention constraint), not a range of correlations, and it is not 'of mind wandering'; Draheim 2021 full mediation (N=396) held only with accuracy-based tasks and needs replication.
claim_before_audit: Attention control (antisaccade, visual arrays) carries much of the WM-Gf link (executive attention view); restraint and constraint of mind wandering correlate .46-.74, not 1.

claim: Pupil-linked LC-NE baseline arousal does NOT predict Gf, WM or attention control in two labs (N=224 for Gf, r=-.01, BF01=11.6); LC-NE theory of individual differences is partly refuted for baseline pupil size.
agent_test: none (human only)

claim: WM training gives near transfer but essentially no far transfer to Gf against active controls: g=0.05 [-0.02,0.13], k=67 (Melby-Lervag 2016); passive vs treated controls differ on nonverbal ability, Q(1)=6.09, p=.01; n-back with treated controls g=0.15 rests on five small single-test studies with control-group drops; Lawlor-Savage 2016 null, BF 39.97:1. Au 2015 (n-back only, 20 studies, adults 18-50) reports a small positive Gf effect; the disagreement is explained by control type, baseline correction and scope. Au's own g=0.24 and the 'about 0.13 active' figure were not re-read.
schema_part: none (change the scaffold, not the capacity)
agent_test: Compare scaffolding vs more practice examples at equal tokens
audit_note: Melby-Lervag numbers, Q(1)=6.09, five n-back studies and Lawlor-Savage BF 39.97 all match; the 'baseline correction' part of the explanation is not shown in opened sources (control type is); Lawlor-Savage ages 30-60 and 57 analysed.

claim: WM explains Gf is not shown to be causal: process overlap fits, and the mediation WM gain -> Gf gain was null (beta=-.01, k=26). Re-read Melby-Lervag 2016: visuospatial WM gain vs nonverbal gain beta=.13, p=.10, k=38. No LLM study tests process overlap vs shared bottleneck.
agent_test: none

claim: Chat LLMs show human-like n-back decline: d-prime falls to about 1 near n=3; spatial lower than verbal; chain-of-thought helps spatial; small open models near floor. Mostly one research group.
agent_test: Run n-back at n=1-6 for the agent with and without a written scratch state
audit_note: The n=3 decline is for GPT-3.5; GPT-4 was only tested to n=3 and far exceeds it, so 'chat LLMs' is slightly wide; Zhang et al. abstract was opened but gave no n-back specifics.

claim: Open-model n-back retrieval collapses from 1-back to 2-back for weak models (Qwen1.5-14B 1.00 -> .09) but scale and curriculum fix it (Llama3.1-70B .99/.93 at 2/3-back; 8-10 back 75-57%, 80-72% with curriculum).
agent_test: Replicate with the agent model at equal tokens; track retrieval accuracy by depth

claim: In small transformers trained from scratch, a 1-layer 1-head model shows a logarithmic accuracy decline up to N=6 while most models with more layers or heads stay above 95%; in 15 pretrained LLMs (70M to 14B) errors cluster on lures (models say match to 79% of N-1 lures at N=2), which Gong 2026 attributes to readout under interference rather than finding the item; Xiong et al. report a 2-layer transformer solves the task perfectly. This points to interference and attention dispersion, not a fixed architectural limit.
schema_part: G do not rely on implicit memory
agent_test: Make the agent restate its rule list each step; measure lure errors
audit_note: Numbers match (most larger models above 95%, not all), but 'limit is architectural' overreaches: Gong 2026 locates it in readout under interference, and the 2-layer perfect solution shows capacity depends on model size/training, not a fixed architectural ceiling; all but Xiong are one author (Gong).
claim_before_audit: The LLM limit is architectural: 1-layer 1-head attention shows a log decline to N=6; deeper or wider models stay above 95%; a readout bottleneck (lure errors 79% at N=2) is shared across 15 models; a 2-layer transformer solves the task perfectly.

claim: N-back accuracy correlates with general benchmarks across 10 open models in non-thinking mode (autoregressive r: MMLU-Pro .78, GPQA Diamond .88, IFEval .69), but log parameter count did not predict them, while in de Langis 2025 parameters vs mean span r=0.82 (p<.05, six models). Benchmarks are knowledge and instruction following, not matrix reasoning; N=10; no size-controlled partial correlation read.
agent_test: n/a

claim: LLMs have near-perfect forward span (50 digits, .99-1.00) but fail backward span at 15 digits (.00-.83) and incongruent Stroop-like control (40-60% vs human 93-96%); explicit reasoning lifts incongruent accuracy to .91-.99.
schema_part: G control over storage; O explicit reasoning
agent_test: Add a reasoning step on manipulation tasks; compare at equal tokens

claim: Instruction density degrades compliance (IFScale, 20 models, 5 runs): best model about 68% at 500 (probably gemini-2.5-pro, inferred from a garbled table); o3 62.8%, grok-3 61.9%, claude-3.7-sonnet 52.7%, claude-opus-4 44.6%, claude-sonnet-4 42.9%, deepseek-r1 30.9%, qwen3 26.9%; reasoning models near-perfect through 100-250; omission is the main error; primacy bias peaks at 150-200 then fades beyond 300. Claude thinking mode gives moderate gains (figure only). A generated YES/NO checklist pass (STICK) adds +3.8 (Command-R+) and +0.8 (GPT-4o) on LiveBench while free-form Self-Refine hurts.
schema_part: G limit live rules, re-check list; O verification
agent_test: Measure compliance vs number of simultaneous rules, with and without a checklist re-pass

claim: Parallel-branch and sequential state tracking show cliffs (100% through 12 parallel branches, collapse at 20-30; entity tracking of changed boxes 3.1% by probe), resembling WM limits. Illusion of Thinking: Hanoi collapse near 7-8 disks even when the algorithm is given; MAKER: with the state rewritten at every step plus voting, 20 disks (1,048,575 steps) ran with zero errors.
agent_test: Chunk the problem into sub-steps at equal tokens and compare cliff location
audit_note: The 3.1% is a probing classifier's accuracy on non-trivial Alchemy cases (from earlier work, as analysed by Kim and Schuster), not a direct LLM measure; 'resembling WM limits' is interpretation.

claim: Self-tracking over a dialogue (twenty questions) fails in most non-reasoning LLMs (GPT-4o-mini failed 200/200); reasoning models (R1 100%, o3-mini 96.7%) succeed; CoT is the repair.
agent_test: Insert a written constraint state per turn and test

claim: On matrix-reasoning tasks LLMs approach humans on simple forms. The headline collapse of o3-mini 86.6% -> 17.0% and R1 80.6 -> 22.8 on I-RAVEN-X is caused mostly by simulated perceptual noise (confounders plus smoothed value distributions), not by longer rows or wider ranges: with clean inputs, range 10 -> 1000 costs o3-mini 5.6 points and R1 gains 2.2. Old LLMs (GPT-4) fall on arithmetic rules as range grows (arithmetic 73.6 -> 8.4). Neuro-symbolic ARLC 98.6 -> 88.0; GPT-3 beat humans on generative analogies (OR 1.88) with fewer rules.
agent_test: Keep rule count fixed, add input uncertainty, compare with and without a verified symbolic state
audit_note: Camposampiero abstract and table say R1 fell to 23.2% (text elsewhere says 22.8%); the 'LLMs approach humans on simple forms' lead sentence is vague but Webb et al. (GPT-3 above 40 students, OR 1.88) supports it; 73.6 is the 3x3 value with per-attribute queries.

claim: Effective context is shorter than claimed: RULER gives effective 64K for GPT-4 and Llama3.1-70B, 32K for Qwen2-72B.
agent_test: Test the agent at long contexts with fixed task difficulty

claim: 591 LLMs show interrelated Gf/Gkn/Grw/Gq factors with a combined knowledge/reading group factor, so psychometric g structure may transfer to LLMs.
agent_test: n/a

claim: Rule-following in reasoning models is limited by procedure execution length, not by knowing the rules: giving the explicit algorithm did not move the Hanoi collapse (about 7-8 disks) and the first error often falls within the first 10-15% of the move sequence.
agent_test: Checkpoint the state every k steps and re-verify; compare the collapse point with and without checkpoints at equal tokens

claim: An explicit external state rewritten at each step removes the length collapse: MAKER solved 1,048,575 Hanoi steps with zero errors using one-step microagents that pass next_state, plus voting. Zhang 2024: a chunked status list lifted Tracking Shuffled Objects to 96.4% (+35.4). Neither study holds tokens equal or varies rule count, so the gap-1 question (does gain scale with rule count at equal tokens) is not answered.
schema_part: S states (written working state), O decomposition
agent_test: Items with 2, 4, 8, 16 interacting rules; state-written vs no-state at equal output tokens; plot gain against rule count

claim: Reasoning-model failure on matrix items comes from uncertain inputs, not from the number of rules or values: more reasoning effort did not rescue it (o3-mini high effort 31.0% at 53,596 tokens, versus 17.0% at medium).
agent_test: Add distractor attributes to rule items; check whether a pre-pass that filters relevant attributes restores accuracy

claim: Arithmetic rules are the weak point of older LLMs on rule items, and splitting the query by attribute (a chunking step) lifts GPT-4 arithmetic accuracy from 27.1% to 73.6%.
agent_test: One query per attribute vs one joint query at equal tokens

claim: Not re-testing rejected hypotheses is predicted by Gf and attention disengagement, not by WMC (Lee and Engle 2026 preprint, abstract only); human work separates holding from disengaging, and no LLM study separates suppressing distractor rules from holding rules.
agent_test: Compare scaffolds with an explicit rejected list vs a longer active-rule list on search tasks

claim: No LLM study tests whether a capacity-type load hits all rule tasks alike (shared bottleneck) or only task-specific ones (process overlap); process overlap theory in humans is supported by network-level connectivity (N=297 study) but gives no LLM prediction without inference.
agent_test: Apply the same load manipulation to several rule tasks; test for one common slope vs task-specific slopes

claim: WM training 0.05 vs 0.24 dispute: Melby-Lervag attributes it to control type (Q=6.09, p=.01), missing baseline adjustment, n-back-only scope and age range in Au; Au's own numbers were not retrieved. Treat far transfer from capacity training as unsupported.
agent_test: none
